title: KV cache compact-rewrite heuristics and stepped reclamation
body:
Purpose and quick summary:

This doc captures a pragmatic design for running background compact-rewrite passes in our KV cache to reduce fragmentation without large stop-the-world operations. The goal is a low-risk, incremental pathway (stepped reclamation) that improves cache density and reduces OOM/pressure events while preserving tail latency SLOs. This is intentionally different from prior slab morphing or generational proposals: it focuses on rewrite heuristics, low-lock background workers, and safe coordination with in-flight requests and the runtime’s kernel execution threads.

Motivation / problems we see in prod:
- Gradual fragmentation observed on dGPU hosts after long-lived deployments; fragmentation correlates with increased page fault rates and higher allocation tail times.
- Large compaction passes cause CPU spikes and occasional 99.9th latency regressions.
- Existing eviction heuristics are good for churn but struggle when many mid-sized entries create unusable free gaps.
- Customers with long prefix reuse pay penalties because small free runs prevent placement of compressed/quantized large entries.

Design goals:
1) Reduce fragmentation over time with bounded CPU and lock contention.
2) Avoid global stop-the-world compaction; maintain steady-state SLOs.
3) Provide tunable knobs per-deployment (Dedicated vs Hosted).
4) Emit signals and metrics that enable automated tuning by Redwood Optimize.

Key concepts / terminology:
- rewrite-unit: contiguous region we attempt to coalesce/defragment by copying live entries out and coalescing free space. Typical size: 64KB-1MB depending on host type.
- ghost-entry: tombstoned or logically-evicted item still occupying physical space due to delayed reclamation (e.g., pinned by in-flight requests).
- step-window: time window where a background worker can perform N rewrite-units without exceeding CPU budget.

Worker model:
- Per-NUMA background worker threads with priority lanes: low-priority (always-on, small budget), opportunistic (stepped-in under low CPU), and emergency (triggered when free-heap < threshold).
- Each worker picks candidate segments based on a 'fragmentation score' (see below), attempts lock-free read-snapshot of headers, and then copies live values into a local staging buffer.
- Once staging completes, a CAS operation swaps new pointers and frees the old region. If CAS fails (due to concurrent mutation), the worker aborts and schedules a re-eval later.

Fragmentation scoring and candidate selection:
We compute a lightweight score per region updated by allocation/free events and sampled by prometheus counters:
- free-run-ratio = largest_free_run / region_size (weighted)
- live-density = live_bytes / region_size
- ghost-ratio = ghost_bytes / region_size
- age-factor = time_since_last_compact (exponential backoff)
Final score = a*free-run-ratio + b*(1-live-density) + c*ghost-ratio + d*age-factor (configurable weights).
Only regions with score > threshold are eligible for rewrite passes. Sampling intervals: workers poll hot region candidates every 30s; full scan once per host per 6h for long-tail.

Locking and safety:
- Header metadata uses atomics for occupancy and a generation counter. A rewrite pass reads header+generation, copies entries, then does a single generation CAS to swap in new subregion descriptor.
- Pinned references (requests holding KV references) increment a lightweight pin counter. Workers will skip entries with pin counter > 0 or will make a best-effort to replicate but not free the old space until pin drops.
- In-flight readers continue to follow old pointers; old memory freed only after epoch reclamation (grace period). We reuse existing epoch-manager used by model KV cache.

Memory pool interactions and reclaimed flows:
- Stepped reclamation integrates with pool-allocator by returning reclaimed whole regions (not individual small fragments) to free lists. This prevents allocator churn and helps coalesce.
- Worker will prefer to rebuild regions into contiguous placement within the same pool and NUMA domain. If not possible, it may relocate to a different pool but then marks region as 'moved' to allow routing knobs to prefer in-domain allocations next time.

CPU budgeting and throttling:
- Each host exposes a compaction_cpu_budget_pct (default 2%) for low priority workers and a burst budget (default additional 8%) for opportunistic passes when CPU idle > 30s.
- Workers maintain a compacted_bytes/second metric; autoscaler uses this to tune budgets per host class.

Telemetry and observability:
Emit these metrics per-region and aggregated per-host:
- region_fragmentation_score
- compact_rewrites_attempted / succeeded / aborted
- compact_cpu_millis_consumed
- ghost_bytes, pinned_entry_count
- average_free_run_length
- allocation_failures_due_to_fragmentation
Also surface events to tracing for heavy compaction passes and record associated model-inference request traces when compaction coincides with latency spikes.

API surface and operator knobs:
- runtime config: compact.enabled, compact.cpu_pct, compact.step_window_ms, compact.size_hint, compact.max_retries
- per-customer override in Dedicated: allow aggressive compact schedules for low-latency sensitive customers under commit.

Rollout plan (safe incremental):
1) Canary: enable low-priority workers on 5% of Dedicated hosts with compaction_cpu_budget_pct=0.5% and very conservative thresholds. Monitor allocation_failures and 99.9 latency for 2 weeks.
2) Increase to 25% with slightly higher budget (1%) and add ghost_bytes gauge to dashboards.
3) Enable opportunistic lane in 10% of hosts; run experiments to measure compaction throughput and effect on fragmentation over 30 days.
4) Gradual wide rollout with tuning exposed in Redwood Console + Optimize recommendations.

Open questions / risks:
- CAS window size: aggressive copying may increase CAS contention on highly-updated keys. We should measure conflict rate in benchmark harness.
- Worst-case recovery path: if many aborted compaction attempts pile up, we risk thrashing. Consider backoff/backpressure heuristics per-region.
- Interaction with quantized static allocations: moving a quantized model checkpoint slice may be expensive; we should provide an exclusion list for pinned model segments.
- Precision of fragmentation scoring: choose cheap-to-compute signals to avoid adding overhead.

Experiments to run (bench harness ideas):
- Synthetic mix: 70% short-lived, 20% mid-sized, 10% long-lived entries; measure free-run distribution over 7 days with and without stepped reclamation.
- Read-pinned stress: simulate long-running in-flight references and measure ghost ratio and reclaim latency.
- CAS conflict stress: high update rate on small keys in compacted region to see abort rate.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Prototype: implement per-NUMA worker + generation CAS in a feature branch (PR linked above). Lena to own initial benchmark harness.
- Add metrics to host exporter and a minimal dashboard. Marco to add prometheus metrics and alert for allocation_failures_due_to_fragmentation.
- Validate epoch reclamation correctness with workload that pins KV views for 10s. Samir to run.
- Draft a short runbook for oncall describing how to drain compaction workers and toggle budgets per-host.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is deliberately pragmatic: we prioritise incremental, observable improvements that can be tuned. Avoid designing a single giant compaction sweep for now.
- Feedback wanted on scoring formula and safe CAS swap semantics (is a single-gen counter enough or do we need a versioned double-compare?).

References:
- INF-1293 (Jira) contains initial outage timeline caused by fragmentation on p4d hosts.
- internal/bench/kv-fragmentation folder contains raw harness and traces (see linked PR).
- prior proposals focused on slab morphing and generational evacuation; this doc aims to complement those approaches with a lower-risk worker approach.

---- end of doc ----
